summary: Deep technical session focused on integrating OpenTelemetry token-level traces and metrics into Valkyrie Systems' private Redwood deployment. Covered span design, sampling vs aggregation, cardinality control, KV cache visibility, batching/backpressure behavior, quantization impact on perf, and dashboarding for SLOs. Action items to share examples and run a short microbenchmark in their VPC.
topics: OTEL span design for token-level tracing
KV cache observability and cache hit instrumentation
VPC/private deployment constraints and security logging
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for carving out time. Maya from Redwood - AE. Quick intros?
[00:08] Anika Patel: Hi I'm Anika, platform eng on Valkyrie infra, managing the private cluster and observability.
[00:12] Ralph Nguyen: Ralph, SRE. We run the ingress and long term traces.
[00:16] Priya Shah: Priya, head of ML infra, owning serving and cost.
[00:20] Diego Alvarez: Diego here, SE, I'll drive the perf stuff.
[00:23] Samir Bose: Samir, security.
[00:25] Emily Carter: Emily, app dev, will own dashboarding for product.
[00:28] Maya Chen: Awesome. Goal for today: concrete plan for OTEL + token telemetry with low-cardinality metrics, plus how Redwood runtime exposes KV cache and batching signals in a private VPC.
[00:40] Priya Shah: High level first: our constraints are strict network egress, 90 day logs retention on-prem, and we want token-level insights but worried about cardinality and ingest cost.
[00:52] Diego Alvarez: Totally fair. We usually recommend a hybrid approach: fine-grained token traces for sampling and aggregated token-level metrics. We'll show span examples and how to compute token latency histograms without exploding cardinality.
[01:05] Ralph Nguyen: When you say token-level metrics, is that per-token counters or aggregated per-request histograms?
[01:10] Diego Alvarez: Good question. We prefer aggregations: e.g., per-request token count, per-model per-second token rate, and sampled token spans for hot path debugging. Avoid attaching the token index as a label.
[01:22] Anika Patel: What about streaming responses? Our app streams partial tokens to clients - we need to correlate stream latency and backend runtime batch latencies.
[01:31] Diego Alvarez: For streaming, we emit two spans: generation_span and emit_span. generation_span covers runtime generation and KV cache hits; emit_span wraps the network send to the client. Keep them correlated via trace_id. That avoids per-token labels while letting you measure end-to-end stream tail latency.
[01:45] Maya Chen: We'll drop an example proto and a recommended attribute set after the call.
[01:49] Emily Carter: Could you show how tags/attributes look?
[01:53] Diego Alvarez: Sure, example attributes: model_id, model_variant, request_size_tokens, response_size_tokens, batch_id (but not token_index), cache_hit_ratio (percent), kv_cache_keys_accessed_count, quantization_flag. We also include a boolean fallback_flag when a request falls back to another model.
[02:15] Priya Shah: About batch_id - if we put it on every span won't that create cardinality surges?
[02:20] Diego Alvarez: It can. We avoid using high-cardinality batch_id in long-term metrics; instead it's useful in traces. For metrics we publish sampled batch_latency_{p50,p95,p99} aggregated per model and per deployment pool.
[02:35] Anika Patel: How do you suggest measuring KV cache effectiveness? We have an in-memory cache layer and want to know if KV cache is providing real token reuse.
[02:43] Diego Alvarez: Two signals: 1) metric: kv_cache_hit_ratio by model and tenant (low-card labels), 2) trace attribute: kv_keys_touched (int) and a short sampled trace that includes the actual key counts. For dashboards we recommend a heatmap of kv_cache_hit_ratio vs request prefix length.
[03:02] Ralph Nguyen: That heatmap idea—how do we compute prefix length? We don't want to log full content.
[03:08] Diego Alvarez: Compute prefix_length as token_count_prefetched or token_prefix_len bucketed: 0-8,9-32,33-128. Only publish bucket name as label. No textual content avoids PII leakage.
[03:20] Samir Bose: Security check: is any PII ever attached to spans?
[03:24] Maya Chen: Redwood does not recommend sending user text in OTEL attributes. Use counts and buckets only. We'll include our privacy checklist in the security docs.
[03:32] Samir Bose: Okay send that.
[03:34] Priya Shah: Backpressure: during high load we see queueing upstream. How does Redwood surface queue lengths and backpressure events?
[03:42] Diego Alvarez: The runtime exposes metrics: request_queue_length per-pool, inflight_requests, per-second token_emitted_rate, and backpressure_events_total with labels reason: capacity|kv_lock|io. We also emit a backpressure_span when a request is paused longer than threshold.
[03:58] Priya Shah: Is backpressure span high-cardinality? It will be per-request with trace id.
[04:03] Diego Alvarez: Spans are sampled; backpressure spans are a target for 1% sampling by default in production. Metrics still aggregate counts.
[04:12] Emily Carter: For dashboards, we like to show end-to-end P95 in one panel alongside backend generation P95 and emit P95. Any recommended panel layouts?
[04:21] Lena Park: We ship a starter Grafana dashboard JSON that maps to the metrics I mentioned. We'll attach that and a lightweight Loki query for trace IDs correlated to errors.
[04:31] Maya Chen: We'll share the dashboard. Diego, can you explain quantization signals? We've heard quantized models reduce latency but occasionally increase tail latency due to kernel variance.
[04:41] Diego Alvarez: Short answer: quantization reduces avg token latency and GPU memory utilization but it can increase variability for certain sequence lengths and model architectures. We add quantized=true attribute and expose quant_latency_histogram. Also we publish kernel_switch_events_total to record when runtime switches kernel paths (int -> float fallback). That helps debug tail spikes.
[05:05] Priya Shah: We run on private GPUs with strict driver versions. How sensitive is kernel switching to CUDA/CuDNN versions?
[05:12] Diego Alvarez: Very sensitive. We maintain a compatibility matrix. In private deployments we provide a small shim that reports kernel compatibility and suggests pinned drivers. We'll include this in the private deployment checklist.
[05:24] Anika Patel: On ingest cost: we want to ship metrics to our OTEL collector internal cluster, not to Redwood. Any recommended aggregation to keep ingest rates sane?
[05:33] Diego Alvarez: Aggregate at the collector: generate delta counters rather than per-token increments, and use pre-aggregation for histograms. Also downsample token-level spans to 0.5-1% for full traces, while emitting aggregated per-minute counters at model/tenant granularity.
[05:48] Ralph Nguyen: What's the guidance for retention? We store raw traces 7 days and metrics 90 days; is that typical?
[05:54] Maya Chen: That's a reasonable starting point. We recommend 7-14d for full traces and longer for metrics depending on audit needs. For incident triage longer traces help but cost goes up.
[06:05] Samir Bose: Audit logs: we need signed audit logs for model rollout and admin actions. Can Redwood push admin events into our SIEM?
[06:13] Maya Chen: Yes, we can forward admin audit events to your SIEM over syslog or write to S3 in an encrypted bucket with KMS. We'll include options in the security doc.
[06:22] Emily Carter: A practical use-case: we saw weird P99 spikes correlated to low KV cache hit ratio for long tail customers. How would you debug that with OTEL?
[06:32] Diego Alvarez: Steps: 1) correlate P99 spikes to kv_cache_hit_ratio drop per-pool; 2) pull sampled traces for those windows to look at batch sizes and kernel switches; 3) check backpressure events; 4) examine quantization kernel_switches and model fallbacks.
[06:47] Anika Patel: Can you show a quick example query for the heatmap you mentioned?
[06:51] Diego Alvarez: Example PromQL: sum by (model, prefix_bucket) (rate(kv_cache_hits_total[5m])) / sum by (model, prefix_bucket) (rate(kv_cache_requests_total[5m])) 
[07:05] Anika Patel: Right, we'll adapt that.
[07:09] Priya Shah: Regarding VPC deployment: network egress and cross-AZ latency matter. Does Redwood runtime emit network latency breakdowns?
[07:16] Diego Alvarez: Yes, we emit network_send_latency_histogram and inter-node_rpc_latency_histogram. We also include labels for zone_id when available. That helps identify cross-AZ penalties.
[07:28] Ralph Nguyen: For private air-gapped setups, how do we receive Redwood updates without egress?
[07:34] Maya Chen: We support an offline bundle: signed runtime binary and a telemetry shim that runs locally. The shim can be configured to publish compressed telemetry to a secure internal collector. We'll follow up with the bundle process.
[07:46] Samir Bose: We need to ensure the telemetry shim doesn't leak secrets. Does it support mTLS to our OTEL collector?
[07:51] Diego Alvarez: Yes, it supports mTLS and token based auth. We'll include the config snippet.
[07:58] Emily Carter: On the dashboard side, can we surface token-level cost? We want to map tokens to billing buckets to analyze cost per feature.
[08:06] Maya Chen: Redwood exposes per-token cost_estimate metric that multiplies tokens_generated by model_unit_cost. For private deployments, we let you configure the unit cost. The metric is best-effort; it should be used for trend analysis not invoicing.
[08:22] Priya Shah: A concern: token-level telemetry might expose user intents if we attach prefixes. Confirm no text leaves the cluster.
[08:29] Diego Alvarez: Confirmed. Our recommended attributes strictly avoid text; only counts and bucketing are allowed.
[08:34] Maya Chen: Quick demo snippet: Diego, can you narrate the example span payload and what to search for in traces?
[08:39] Diego Alvarez: (screen short description) generation_span: name=redwood.generation; attributes: model_id=redwood-v1, request_size_tokens=12, response_size_tokens=128, cache_hit_ratio=0.8, kv_keys_touched=3, quantized=true, batch_latency_ms=45. emit_span: name=redwood.emit; attributes: bytes_sent=1024, emit_latency_ms=5. Correlate by trace_id and search for generation_span with batch_latency_ms>200.
[09:10] Anika Patel: Nice. Can you also show a query to find traces where kernel_switch happened?
[09:14] Diego Alvarez: We'll add example logs where kernel_switch_events_total>0 and trace sampling.
[09:18] Priya Shah: About sampling: what's a good starting sampling rate per customer?
[09:22] Diego Alvarez: Start with 0.5-1% for traces cluster-wide, increase to 5% for canaries or problematic tenants. Use dynamic sampling tied to anomalies (e.g., spike in backpressure).
[09:34] Maya Chen: Let's talk alerts: recommended SLOs?
[09:38] Diego Alvarez: Example SLOs: 95% of requests complete within X ms (application SLO), 99% of tokens delivered within Y ms for streaming; kv_cache_hit_ratio > 70% for typical prompt shapes; backpressure_event_rate < 0.1% of requests.
[09:56] Emily Carter: For our product dashboards we want a simple panel: P95 end-to-end latency, backend gen P95, kv_cache_hit_ratio - is that in the starter Grafana?
[10:03] Lena Park: Yes, starter Grafana has those three as a single row. We'll send JSON.
[10:08] Anika Patel: Anything about quantization config we should watch for?
[10:12] Diego Alvarez: Watch token-level variance post-quantization and kernel switch counts. We also recommend testing with the actual prompt distributions you run in prod - quantization regressions often show up only on long-tail prefixes.
[10:24] Priya Shah: Are there any pitfalls people run into when correlating traces and metrics?
[10:29] Diego Alvarez: Timestamp skew, sampling mismatch, and high-cardinality labels are the usual suspects. Use consistent clocks (NTP) and include ingestion timestamps. For sampling mismatch, tag sampled traces with a metrics flag so you can link metrics spikes to sample traces.
[10:44] Maya Chen: We're at about 10 min left. Wrap-up and responsibilities?
[10:48] Maya Chen: Action items recap: Diego to push OTEL examples + dashboard JSON; Maya to push security + private deploy checklist; Anika to provide token distribution and load profile; Diego to run 48h microbenchmark and share numbers.
[10:58] Priya Shah: One more quick question: can Redwood runtime expose per-tenant throttles and quotas as OTEL metrics?
[11:03] Diego Alvarez: Yes: tenant_quota_usage and tenant_throttle_events_total are exposed. We also support per-tenant tagging if you want to route telemetry into tenant-specific Grafana folders.
[11:14] Samir Bose: We'll want the telemetry shim config for mTLS and allowed endpoints.
[11:18] Maya Chen: We'll attach the config example.
[11:20] Emily Carter: Thanks all. This was super useful.
[11:23] Maya Chen: Thanks, will send notes and links. Bye everyone.
[11:26] (call ends)
